what_its_for: Quizartinib is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in adults whose cancer has a specific gene change called FLT3-ITD. It is used together with chemotherapy to treat newly diagnosed AML, or it may be used alone after chemotherapy to help keep the cancer from coming back.
how_to_take: Take quizartinib by mouth once a day, at about the same time each day. You can take it with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, cut, or chew it. If you vomit after taking a dose, do not take an extra dose. Just take your next dose at your regular scheduled time.
dosing: The usual dose is 35.4 mg taken once daily. Your doctor may lower your dose or temporarily stop your medicine if you have certain side effects. Always take exactly the dose your doctor prescribes. Do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and it has been less than 12 hours since your scheduled time, take it as soon as you remember. If it has been more than 12 hours, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store quizartinib tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep the tablets in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine away from moisture, heat, and light. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, Seville oranges, and starfruit while taking this medicine, as they can increase the amount of quizartinib in your blood and raise the risk of side effects. Tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL medicines you take, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements, because many medicines can interact with quizartinib. Avoid starting any new medicines without first checking with your doctor or pharmacist. Women who are pregnant or may become pregnant should not handle crushed or broken tablets. Use effective birth control during treatment and for a period of time after your last dose — ask your doctor how long.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: fast, irregular, or pounding heartbeat or chest pain (this could be a sign of a dangerous heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation); severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or stomach pain; signs of infection such as fever, chills, or sore throat; unusual bleeding or bruising; extreme tiredness or weakness; shortness of breath or trouble breathing; swelling of your ankles, feet, or legs; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you. These may be signs of serious side effects that need immediate medical attention.
when_it_works: Quizartinib works by blocking a faulty protein called FLT3 that helps cancer cells grow. You may not feel it working right away. Your doctor will check your blood counts and do other tests regularly to see how well the medicine is working. It is important to keep taking it as directed, even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Quizartinib can harm an unborn baby. Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. Women who can become pregnant and men with female partners who can become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for some time after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for a period after stopping — ask your doctor for specific guidance. Liver problems: If you have liver problems, your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects, especially heart-related effects. Your doctor will monitor you carefully. Children: Quizartinib is not currently approved for use in children.
